questions.question: Which film has grossed the most money worldwide (as of 2024)?
questions.fun_fact: James Cameron's Avatar grossed over $2.9 billion, making it the highest-grossing film of all time — Cameron also holds third place with Titanic.

questions.question: Which video game is the best-selling of all time?
questions.fun_fact: Minecraft has sold over 300 million copies. It was originally developed by a single person — Swedish developer Markus 'Notch' Persson.

questions.question: Which song was the first YouTube video to reach one billion views?
questions.fun_fact: Gangnam Style hit a billion views in 2012 and actually overflowed YouTube's view counter, which could only count up to 2.1 billion at the time.

questions.question: What was the first fully computer-animated feature film?
questions.fun_fact: Toy Story was released in 1995 and produced by Pixar. Steve Jobs funded the studio and saved it from bankruptcy multiple times before the film became a massive hit.

questions.question: Which band has sold the most albums worldwide?
questions.fun_fact: The Beatles have sold an estimated 600 million records. Their active career lasted only about eight years — from 1962 to 1970.

questions.question: Which TV series holds the record for the most Emmy wins for a drama?
questions.fun_fact: Game of Thrones won 59 Emmys in total. Despite the controversial final season, it remains the most awarded drama series in Emmy history.

questions.question: Which actor was awarded a posthumous Oscar for playing the Joker?
questions.fun_fact: Heath Ledger died in January 2008, six months before The Dark Knight premiered. He locked himself in a hotel room for weeks to prepare for the role.

questions.question: What was Nintendo before it became a video game company?
questions.fun_fact: Nintendo was founded in 1889 and made traditional Japanese hanafuda playing cards. It took nearly 100 years before the company became a video game giant.

questions.question: How was nearly all of Toy Story 2 saved from accidental deletion?

answers.text: A backup on an employee's home computer saved the film
The film had to be completely re-animated
An IT specialist recovered the data

questions.fun_fact: A mistyped delete command wiped 90% of the film's data. Technical director Galyn Susman happened to have a copy on her home computer because she was working from home after having a baby.

questions.question: Which streaming service produced the first series to win an Emmy for Best Drama?
questions.fun_fact: Hulu's The Handmaid's Tale won the first streaming Emmy for Best Drama in 2017. Netflix won many Emmys with The Crown but claimed that award later.

questions.question: Which artist has the most number-one hits on the US Billboard charts?
questions.fun_fact: The Beatles hold the record with 20 number-one hits in the US. On a single day in April 1964, they simultaneously occupied all top 5 spots in the Billboard Hot 100.

questions.question: In which country was Tetris invented?
questions.fun_fact: Tetris was created in 1984 by Alexey Pajitnov at the Computing Centre of the Soviet Academy of Sciences in Moscow.

questions.question: Which animated series has aired continuously on US television since 1989?
questions.fun_fact: The Simpsons is the longest-running American animated primetime series. Matt Groening sketched the characters in just 15 minutes in a producer's waiting room.

questions.question: What was the title of the first video ever uploaded to YouTube?
questions.fun_fact: The 18-second video 'Me at the zoo' shows YouTube co-founder Jawed Karim in front of elephants at San Diego Zoo. It was uploaded on 23 April 2005.

questions.question: Which famous actor turned down the role of Gandalf in The Lord of the Rings?
questions.fun_fact: Sean Connery declined because he didn't understand the screenplay. He was reportedly offered 15% of box office revenues — that would have been over $400 million.

questions.question: Which instrument plays the iconic two-note Jaws theme?
questions.fun_fact: John Williams' two-note motif (E–F) is played by the double basses in the original score, supported by tuba and other low brass.

questions.question: What colour was the original iPhone released in 2007?
questions.fun_fact: Steve Jobs unveiled the first iPhone in January 2007. The prototype on stage kept crashing, so the team carefully ordered the demo to show each feature only once.

questions.question: Which was the first Pixar film to gross over $1 billion worldwide?
questions.fun_fact: Toy Story 3 (2010) was the first Pixar film to cross $1 billion worldwide. The first Disney-distributed film to cross that mark was Pirates of the Caribbean: Dead Man's Chest in 2006.

questions.question: What is the famous Konami Code hidden in many video games?

answers.text: Up, Up, Down, Down, Left, Right, Left, Right, B, A
Left, Right, Left, Right, Up, Down, Up, Down, A, B
Up, Down, Up, Down, Left, Right, B, A, Start

questions.fun_fact: The Konami Code was invented in 1986 by developer Kazuhisa Hashimoto for the game Gradius because he found it too difficult. It now appears in hundreds of games and even websites.

questions.question: Which rapper was a ballet dancer before his music career?
questions.fun_fact: Tupac attended the Baltimore School for the Arts, where he studied ballet, acting, and poetry. He even played the Mouse in a production of The Nutcracker.

questions.question: Which song has the most streams on Spotify (as of 2024)?
questions.fun_fact: Blinding Lights spent over 90 weeks on the Billboard Hot 100 — an absolute record. The Weeknd drew inspiration from 80s synth-pop for the sound.

questions.question: Which country is the Netflix series Squid Game set in?
questions.fun_fact: Squid Game became the most-watched Netflix series ever. Director Hwang Dong-hyuk wrote the screenplay in 2009 but couldn't find a studio willing to produce it for over a decade.

questions.question: Which superhero was originally conceived as a villain?
questions.fun_fact: Wolverine first appeared in 1974 as an opponent of the Hulk. He was intended as a one-off antagonist but became so popular he turned hero and eventually the most iconic X-Men member.

questions.question: Which famous director made the Thriller music video for Michael Jackson?
questions.fun_fact: The Thriller video cost $500,000 — the most expensive music video of its time. At 14 minutes long, it was the first music video inducted into the Library of Congress.

questions.question: Which video game was the first to be played in space?
questions.fun_fact: Cosmonaut Alexander Serebrov took a Game Boy with a Tetris cartridge to the Mir space station in 1993 — the cartridge was later auctioned for $1,220.

questions.question: Which actress has appeared in the most episodes of a single TV series?
questions.fun_fact: Mariska Hargitay has played Olivia Benson in Law & Order: SVU since 1999 — over 500 episodes. Her mother was actress Jayne Mansfield.

questions.question: What was the first word ever sent over the internet?
questions.fun_fact: In 1969, 'Login' was intended to be sent, but the computer crashed after 'L' and 'O'. The internet's first word was an accidental 'Lo' — as in 'Lo and behold'.

questions.question: Which streaming service has the most subscribers worldwide (as of 2024)?
questions.fun_fact: Netflix started in 1997 as a DVD-by-mail rental service. Co-founder Reed Hastings reportedly got the idea after paying a $40 late fee for an Apollo 13 VHS tape.

questions.question: Which Lord of the Rings character was originally scripted to die in the battle at the Black Gate?
questions.fun_fact: Peter Jackson actually filmed scenes of Aragorn fighting Sauron and dying. The sequence was cut because it deviated too far from Tolkien's story.

questions.question: Which musician has won the most Grammy Awards?
questions.fun_fact: Beyoncé has won over 30 Grammys, making her the most decorated artist in Grammy history. She was only nine years old at her first audition.

questions.question: Which social media network was the first to reach one billion users?
questions.fun_fact: Facebook hit one billion monthly active users in 2012. Mark Zuckerberg coded the first version in just two weeks in his Harvard dorm room.

questions.question: What is the name of the fictional language created for Game of Thrones?
questions.fun_fact: Linguist David J. Peterson created Dothraki with over 4,000 words and its own grammar. He beat out 30 other applicants who also wanted to develop the language.

questions.question: Which famous fictional character is described as dark-haired in the books but was portrayed as blonde in several films?
questions.fun_fact: In Ian Fleming's novels, James Bond has black hair. Daniel Craig in 2006's Casino Royale was the first blonde film Bond — fans of the books were initially up in arms.

questions.question: Which famous meme came from a photo of a perpetually grumpy-looking cat?
questions.fun_fact: Grumpy Cat (real name Tardar Sauce) had feline dwarfism, which caused her permanently grumpy expression. Her owner reportedly earned over $100 million from the cat.

questions.question: How many books are in the Harry Potter series?
questions.fun_fact: J.K. Rowling was rejected by 12 publishers before Bloomsbury published Harry Potter. The editor only agreed because his eight-year-old daughter loved the first chapter.

questions.question: Which actor has appeared in the most Marvel Cinematic Universe films?
questions.fun_fact: Samuel L. Jackson appeared as Nick Fury in over 11 MCU films. He signed an unprecedented nine-film contract with Marvel — the longest actor contract in Hollywood history.

questions.question: What is true about the first emoji ever created?

answers.text: It was part of a set of 176 emojis

questions.fun_fact: The first 176 emojis were designed in 1999 by Japanese designer Shigetaka Kurita for mobile carrier NTT DoCoMo. Each emoji was only 12×12 pixels. The originals are now displayed in New York's MoMA.

questions.question: Which legendary video game character was named after the landlord of a Nintendo warehouse?
questions.fun_fact: Mario was named after Mario Segale, the landlord of Nintendo's US warehouse. Segale once stormed in demanding overdue rent — and inadvertently inspired the world's most famous game character.

questions.question: Which film was the first to be released with the Dolby Atmos sound system?
questions.fun_fact: Pixar's Brave was the first theatrical film with Dolby Atmos in 2012. The system uses up to 128 separate audio channels and can position sounds three-dimensionally in a room.

questions.question: Which famous musician worked as a part-time baggage handler before becoming famous?
questions.fun_fact: Freddie Mercury worked at London's Heathrow Airport as a baggage handler and sold second-hand clothes at Kensington Market before Queen broke through.

questions.question: Which word was Oxford Dictionary's 'Word of the Year' in 2013?
questions.fun_fact: Usage of the word 'selfie' rose 17,000% in 2013. The oldest known selfie actually dates back to 1839 — a photograph taken by chemist Robert Cornelius.

questions.question: How many seasons did the original Star Trek series have?
questions.fun_fact: The original series ran for only three seasons (1966–1969) and was cancelled due to poor ratings. It became a cult hit in reruns and launched a multi-billion-dollar franchise.

questions.question: Which Hollywood star was a bodybuilder and won the Mr. Universe title before becoming an actor?
questions.fun_fact: Arnold Schwarzenegger won his first Mr. Universe title at just 20 years old. He sometimes trained so hard he passed out in the gym.

questions.question: What colour was the dress that divided the internet in 2015 (#TheDress)?

answers.text: It was actually blue and black
It was actually white and gold
It was actually blue and brown

questions.fun_fact: The viral dress phenomenon of 2015 was studied by scientists and published in academic journals. The differing perceptions arise from how the brain compensates for ambient lighting.

questions.question: In Star Wars, which actor wore the Darth Vader suit while James Earl Jones provided the voice?
questions.fun_fact: British bodybuilder David Prowse only learned his lines wouldn't be used when he saw the finished film — he hadn't been told the voice would be dubbed and was reportedly furious in the screening.

questions.question: What everyday object did the Star Wars lightsaber sound effect originate from?

answers.text: An idling film projector mixed with TV interference
An electric razor on a metal plate

questions.fun_fact: Sound designer Ben Burtt accidentally created the hum when his microphone picked up a broken TV near a running projector. He then waved the mic past a speaker to add the swoosh on movement.

questions.question: What is the asking price for the head of the Hollywood Sign letters that were sold off in the 1980s?

answers.text: Each letter was sponsored by a donor for around $27,000
The letters were given away for free
Each letter sold for over $1 million

questions.fun_fact: When the rotting 1923 sign was replaced in 1978, each of the nine letters was sponsored for $27,777. Hugh Hefner bought the Y, Alice Cooper sponsored an O in memory of Groucho Marx, and Andy Williams bought the W.

questions.question: Which famous movie line was almost entirely improvised?

answers.text: 'I'm the king of the world!' in Titanic
'May the Force be with you' in Star Wars
'Here's looking at you, kid' in Casablanca

questions.fun_fact: James Cameron came up with the line on set after shouting it himself in frustration during pre-production. Leonardo DiCaprio thought it was corny but delivered it anyway — it became one of cinema's most quoted lines.

questions.question: What was the original ending of the 1982 film Blade Runner that test audiences hated?

answers.text: Deckard's voice-over narration explaining the plot
Deckard being killed by a replicant
Rachael being revealed as the villain

questions.fun_fact: Harrison Ford reportedly hated the voice-over and tried to deliberately read it badly so the studio would drop it. The Director's Cut released in 1992 removed it entirely.

questions.question: Which Oscar-winning film was almost titled 'Three Thousand'?
questions.fun_fact: The original 'Three Thousand' was a dark drama about a drug-addicted sex worker who is dumped at the end. Disney bought the script and turned it into a romantic comedy — the title referred to her weekly fee.

questions.question: What unusual thing did Andy Serkis do to prepare for playing Gollum?

answers.text: He observed his cat coughing up hairballs
He lived in a cave for a month

questions.fun_fact: Serkis based Gollum's iconic raspy voice partly on his cat's hairball noises. He was originally hired only to voice the character but ended up performing it in motion capture, revolutionising the technique.

questions.question: What was the original profession of the actor who played Chewbacca?
questions.fun_fact: Peter Mayhew was 7'3" and worked as a porter at a London hospital when Star Wars producers spotted him. He was reportedly hired because he was the only person who could stand up without help when asked during the casting.

questions.question: What was unusual about the production of the 1999 film The Blair Witch Project?

answers.text: The actors were given daily notes telling them where to go but no script
It was shot entirely in a Hollywood studio
All dialogue was recorded after filming

questions.fun_fact: The actors really got lost in the Maryland woods, ate dwindling rations, and were genuinely cold and frustrated. Made for around $60,000, it earned nearly $250 million worldwide.

questions.question: Which sitcom finale was watched live by more US viewers than any other scripted episode in history?
questions.fun_fact: The 1983 M*A*S*H finale drew about 106 million viewers on CBS. New York City reported a major spike in water usage right after the broadcast as millions flushed at once.

questions.question: What did the cast of Friends each earn per episode in the final two seasons?
questions.fun_fact: The six leads negotiated as a single block from season three onward, refusing to take pay raises unless all received the same — a strategy still cited as a Hollywood case study in collective bargaining.

questions.question: What breed of dog is Scooby-Doo?
questions.fun_fact: Scooby's name came from the scat lyric 'doo-be-doo-be-doo' in Frank Sinatra's 'Strangers in the Night'. Producer Fred Silverman heard it on a flight and used it to lock in the character's final name.

questions.question: What was the very first TV commercial ever broadcast in the United States?
questions.fun_fact: The 10-second Bulova spot aired on 1 July 1941 before a Brooklyn Dodgers game on WNBT in New York. It cost the company about $9 to air.

questions.question: Which long-running TV show's pilot featured a completely different lead actor before being recast?
questions.fun_fact: The unaired 2006 pilot had different actresses playing Penny (then called Katie) and an entirely different female lead. CBS rejected it, the creators rewrote, and the recast 2007 pilot launched a 12-season run.

questions.question: Which TV show is famous for its theme song that contains no lyrics, just whistling?
questions.fun_fact: The theme, 'The Fishin' Hole', actually has lyrics, but only the whistled version was used on TV. Andy Griffith himself sang the lyrical version on a later album release.

questions.question: Which classic cocktail surged in popularity in the US after being featured as Don Draper's signature drink on Mad Men?
questions.fun_fact: Don Draper's signature drink turned an old-man cocktail into a hipster staple — bartenders across the US reported Old Fashioned orders rising over 40% during the show's run.

questions.question: Which famous TV character was never shown from the waist down in their entire run?

answers.text: Wilson on Home Improvement (always behind a fence)

questions.fun_fact: Neighbour Wilson was always shown with his face partially hidden behind the backyard fence. In the series finale, the cast finally revealed his full face during a curtain call — the actor was Earl Hindman.

questions.question: Which Beatles album was the first to feature lyrics printed on its sleeve?

answers.text: Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band

questions.fun_fact: Released in 1967, Sgt. Pepper's was the first major rock album to print full lyrics on the back cover — at the time considered a radical artistic gesture treating pop songs like poetry.

questions.question: What is the longest song ever to top the Billboard Hot 100?

answers.text: Taylor Swift's 'All Too Well (10 Minute Version)'

questions.fun_fact: At 10 minutes 13 seconds, Swift's 2021 re-recording broke a record held since 1972 by 'American Pie' (8:42). The original 'All Too Well' from 2012 was about half that length.

questions.question: Which iconic instrument did Jimi Hendrix famously play right-handed-strung but flipped upside down?
questions.fun_fact: Hendrix was left-handed but learned on right-handed guitars by flipping them. This put the controls and tremolo above the strings — and shifted the angled pickup, giving his Strat its distinctive tone.

questions.question: What was unusual about Queen's 'Bohemian Rhapsody' when it was released in 1975?

answers.text: At nearly six minutes, radio executives said it was far too long for a single
It was the first song recorded entirely a cappella
It was released only on vinyl, never on cassette

questions.fun_fact: EMI tried to make Queen cut the song down. Freddie Mercury refused and gave a copy to DJ Kenny Everett, who played it 14 times in two days — public demand forced the full release.

questions.question: Which musician played all the instruments on their multi-platinum debut album?

answers.text: Lenny Kravitz on Let Love Rule

questions.fun_fact: Prince was 19 when he produced, arranged, composed and played all 27 instruments on For You. His Warner Bros. contract giving him full creative control was unprecedented for an unknown artist.

questions.question: On what occasion did ABBA first publicly perform 'Dancing Queen'?

answers.text: A New Year's Eve TV special

questions.fun_fact: ABBA played 'Dancing Queen' on 18 June 1976 at a televised gala the night before the wedding of Sweden's King Carl XVI Gustaf — months before the song's official commercial release.

questions.question: What does the band name ABBA stand for?

answers.text: The initials of the four members' first names
A reference to a Stockholm street

questions.fun_fact: ABBA stands for Agnetha, Björn, Benny, and Anni-Frid. The name was also conveniently the name of a Swedish fish-canning company, which gave permission for the band to use it.

questions.question: Which artist released the first commercially available CD album?

answers.text: The Bee Gees — Saturday Night Fever

questions.fun_fact: Released in Japan in October 1982, Billy Joel's 52nd Street was the first commercial CD pressing. The first players cost around $1,000 — about $3,000 in today's money.

questions.question: What was Pac-Man's original name in Japan before its US release?
questions.fun_fact: Namco changed the name for the US because they feared vandals would easily scratch the 'P' on arcade cabinets into something obscene. The character's name came from the Japanese onomatopoeia 'paku-paku' for the sound of opening and closing your mouth.

questions.question: Why does Mario wear a hat and overalls?

answers.text: Hardware limits made hair and shirt-arms hard to animate
Designer Shigeru Miyamoto thought plumbers looked cool
He was originally a circus performer

questions.fun_fact: On the Donkey Kong arcade in 1981, sprites were tiny and Nintendo couldn't realistically animate hair flowing or arms with sleeves moving against a shirt. A hat solved hair; overalls made arm movement visible against a coloured body.

questions.question: Which game console had a notorious 'red ring of death' hardware failure?
questions.fun_fact: The failure rate was estimated at over 50% in early units. Microsoft eventually took a $1.15 billion charge in 2007 to cover warranty repairs — one of the largest hardware recalls in gaming history.

questions.question: Which 1993 game is widely credited with inventing the first-person shooter genre as we know it?
questions.fun_fact: id Software's Doom built on 1992's Wolfenstein 3D but added textured floors, varied heights and multiplayer 'deathmatch' — a word id co-founder John Romero coined. Within two years it was installed on more PCs than Windows.

questions.question: Why did the Atari 2600 game E.T. become legendary?

answers.text: It was so bad that unsold copies were buried in a New Mexico landfill
It was the first video game to win an Oscar
It crashed every NASA computer of the 1980s

questions.fun_fact: Made in just six weeks to meet the 1982 Christmas rush, E.T. is often blamed for the 1983 video game crash. The landfill burial was confirmed in 2014 when archaeologists excavated thousands of cartridges in Alamogordo.

questions.question: What error number became infamous on Diablo III's 2012 launch day?
questions.fun_fact: 'Error 37' meant Blizzard's servers were full, locking players out of an always-online game they had paid for. The message became a meme and forced Blizzard to apologise publicly within days.

questions.question: What was the name of the first arcade video game ever sold commercially?
questions.fun_fact: Computer Space was designed by Nolan Bushnell, who went on to found Atari. It flopped commercially because players found the controls too complex — Bushnell learned from this and made Pong dead simple.

questions.question: What was Stan Lee's signature catchphrase, used on countless Marvel comic pages?
questions.fun_fact: Lee chose 'Excelsior!' — Latin for 'ever upward' and the New York state motto — because he wanted a sign-off no other writer was using. He cameoed in over 30 Marvel films.

questions.question: Which superhero was inspired by a real person — the writer's wife?
questions.fun_fact: Psychologist William Moulton Marston created Wonder Woman in 1941 inspired by his wife Elizabeth and their partner Olive Byrne, who both championed early feminist ideas. Marston also helped invent the lie-detector — which became Wonder Woman's Lasso of Truth.

questions.question: Which comic book superhero made his debut in Detective Comics #27 in 1939?
questions.fun_fact: DC stands for Detective Comics — named after the very title that introduced Batman. Co-creator Bill Finger fought for decades to receive credit alongside Bob Kane and was officially acknowledged by DC only in 2015.

questions.question: In which TV show did the Marvel character X-23 first appear before crossing into films?
questions.fun_fact: X-23 (Laura Kinney) was created by Craig Kyle and Christopher Yost for the 2003 animated series as Wolverine's female clone. She crossed into live action in 2017's Logan, played by Dafne Keen.

questions.question: What was the very first item ever sold on eBay in 1995?
questions.fun_fact: Founder Pierre Omidyar emailed the winning bidder to make sure he understood the laser pointer was broken. The buyer replied that he collected broken laser pointers — that was the moment Omidyar realised eBay would work.

questions.question: Which dance craze went viral after a music video by South Korean artist PSY?
questions.fun_fact: PSY based the horse-trot dance on his idea of how a wealthy Gangnam district resident would dance ironically. The 2012 video kicked off K-pop's mainstream global breakthrough.

questions.question: What was the original purpose of the @ symbol used in email addresses?

answers.text: It was a commercial shorthand for 'at the price of'
It was invented in 1971 specifically for email
It started as a medieval scribal abbreviation for 'and'

questions.fun_fact: The @ sign was used by merchants for centuries before computer programmer Ray Tomlinson picked it in 1971 to separate user from machine in email addresses — he wanted a character that wouldn't appear in any name.

questions.question: What does 'GIF' stand for, and how does its creator say it's pronounced?

answers.text: Graphics Interchange Format — pronounced 'JIF' according to its creator
General Image File — pronounced with a hard G

questions.fun_fact: Steve Wilhite, who created the format at CompuServe in 1987, insisted on the soft-G pronunciation, even joking it was 'jraphics interchange format'. Most of the internet still says it the other way.

questions.question: Which website did Mark Zuckerberg launch before Facebook that landed him in disciplinary trouble at Harvard?
questions.fun_fact: In 2003, Zuckerberg scraped student photos from Harvard's online house directories without permission and let users rank them by attractiveness. The site received 22,000 page views in its first four hours and was shut down within days.

questions.question: What was Reddit originally going to be — before pivoting in its first week?

answers.text: A food-ordering app for mobile phones

questions.fun_fact: Steve Huffman and Alexis Ohanian originally pitched 'My Mobile Menu' to Y Combinator in 2005 and were rejected. Paul Graham told them to build something else — they came up with Reddit in 48 hours.

questions.question: Which iconic clothing item was originally designed as durable workwear for miners and labourers?
questions.fun_fact: Levi Strauss & Jacob Davis patented the riveted denim trouser in 1873 for California Gold Rush miners. The copper rivets at stress points were the actual innovation in the patent — not the fabric itself.

questions.question: Why does the little Ralph Lauren polo logo show a polo player?

answers.text: Lauren wanted to evoke aristocratic 'old money' sportswear
Lauren himself was a professional polo player
The logo was bought from an actual British polo club

questions.fun_fact: Ralph Lauren (born Ralph Lifshitz) had never played polo. He picked the sport because it was associated with English aristocracy — exactly the world his brand sold to upwardly mobile American customers.

questions.question: Which luxury fashion house started by selling leather travel trunks in Paris?
questions.fun_fact: Louis Vuitton opened his trunk-maker shop in 1854. His flat-topped trunks were a revolution — previous trunks had domed lids to shed rain, but flat tops could be stacked for train and ship travel.

questions.question: What did Coco Chanel revolutionise in women's fashion in the 1920s?

answers.text: She popularised trousers, jersey fabric and the 'little black dress' for women
She designed the first wedding dress in white

questions.fun_fact: Chanel used jersey — previously a men's underwear fabric — to make comfortable women's daywear. Her 1926 'little black dress' was nicknamed 'Chanel's Ford' by Vogue because it would be as universal as the Model T.

questions.question: What did Michael Jordan reportedly insist on changing every game during his career?

answers.text: He wore his University of North Carolina shorts under his Bulls uniform
He demanded a new ball for every quarter

questions.fun_fact: Jordan wore his lucky UNC shorts under every game uniform — which is also why NBA shorts got longer in the 1990s: he needed his Bulls shorts cut bigger to fit over the college pair.

questions.question: For what unusual category did the modern Olympics award medals from 1912 to 1948?

answers.text: Painting, sculpture and other fine arts

questions.fun_fact: Pierre de Coubertin, founder of the modern Olympics, insisted on medals for painting, sculpture, architecture, literature and music. About 151 medals were awarded across seven Games before the IOC ended the practice.

questions.question: What did the Wimbledon tennis tournament traditionally insist all players wear?
questions.fun_fact: The rule dates to the Victorian era when visible sweat stains were considered scandalous — white showed sweat least. The All England Club still enforces it, with strict guidelines on the thickness of any non-white trim.

questions.question: What was Lady Gaga's career before she became a global pop star?

answers.text: She worked as a songwriter for other artists at Interscope
She was a child actress on Broadway
She was a competitive figure skater

questions.fun_fact: Before her solo breakthrough, Gaga wrote songs for Britney Spears, the Pussycat Dolls and Fergie. She was dropped from her first label, Def Jam, after only three months in 2006.

questions.question: Which Golden Age Hollywood actress co-invented a frequency-hopping radio technology used in modern Wi-Fi?
questions.fun_fact: The Austrian-American actress patented a frequency-hopping system in 1942 to prevent jamming of Allied torpedoes. The underlying idea is a foundation of modern Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and GPS.

questions.question: What did Keanu Reeves famously do after the success of The Matrix sequels?

answers.text: He gave large portions of his back-end pay to the costume and effects crew
He bought every cast member a Porsche
He retired from acting for five years

questions.fun_fact: Reeves reportedly redirected an estimated $75–100 million of his Matrix back-end profits to the special effects and costume departments, saying they were what really made the films work.

questions.question: Which pop star's tour rider is known to require humidifiers in every dressing room to protect her voice?
questions.fun_fact: Carey's riders famously demand humidifiers, a specific temperature range, and quiet time before shows. She calls her cords her 'precious instruments' and reportedly avoids speaking on show days to save her range.

questions.question: Which famous actor was a professional clown before getting into film?
questions.fun_fact: Brosnan trained as a fire-eater and circus clown in London in his late teens before turning to acting. He performed in the streets and at children's parties to make ends meet.

questions.question: Which famous talk-show host kept the same band leader for 25 years?
questions.fun_fact: Severinsen led the NBC Orchestra on The Tonight Show from 1967 to 1992. His flamboyant suits became a running joke — Carson once said Severinsen looked like 'a Las Vegas pimp' on national TV.

questions.question: Why was the bubble-wrap that became a global packaging staple originally invented?

answers.text: It was meant to be sold as textured wallpaper
It was designed as insulation for spacecraft
It was created as a children's pool float

questions.fun_fact: Engineers Alfred Fielding and Marc Chavannes sealed two shower curtains together in 1957 hoping to sell trendy wallpaper. That flopped, a greenhouse-insulation pitch flopped too, and only when IBM needed to protect a new computer in shipping did the product find its calling.

questions.question: Why do CDs and DVDs read data using a laser instead of a needle like a vinyl record?

answers.text: The laser reads microscopic pits without ever touching the disc
The laser physically burns a new groove on every play
The laser magnetises the surface to store sound

questions.fun_fact: A CD stores data as a spiral of tiny pits and flat 'lands'. The laser detects how light reflects differently off pits versus lands. Because nothing touches the surface, a CD doesn't wear out from playing the way a vinyl record does under its needle.

questions.question: Why does a microwave oven heat food but the plate often stays cool?

answers.text: The waves excite water molecules, and most plates contain little water
The plate reflects all the microwaves back upward
The plate is coated to block heat absorption

questions.fun_fact: Microwaves make water molecules flip back and forth billions of times a second, and that friction is the heat. Ceramic and glass have almost no water to wobble, so they only get warm by contact with the hot food, not from the microwaves themselves.

questions.question: Why do glow-in-the-dark stars keep shining after you turn off the light?

answers.text: They slowly release stored light energy as a delayed glow
They contain a tiny battery that powers a faint bulb
They react chemically with oxygen in the dark

questions.fun_fact: This is called phosphorescence. The material absorbs light and traps that energy in its atoms, then leaks it back out slowly over minutes. It's the same principle behind old watch dials, just without the radioactive paint that early ones used.

questions.question: Why does a fizzy drink suddenly foam over when you drop a mint candy into it?

answers.text: The candy's rough surface gives trapped gas thousands of escape points
The mint chemically reacts with the cola to create new gas
The candy lowers the liquid's temperature, releasing gas

questions.fun_fact: The soda is packed with dissolved carbon dioxide desperate to escape. A mint's pitted, bumpy surface offers countless tiny sites where bubbles can form at once, so the gas erupts all together. It's physics, not a chemical reaction at all.

questions.question: Why does popcorn pop?

answers.text: Water trapped inside turns to steam and bursts the hard shell
The sugar inside the kernel caramelises and expands
Air pockets in the kernel ignite from the heat

questions.fun_fact: Each kernel holds a droplet of water inside a starchy centre and a tough waterproof hull. Heated past boiling, the water becomes steam under pressure until the hull fails explosively, turning the starch inside out into the fluffy shape you eat.

questions.question: Why do helium balloons make your voice sound squeaky?

answers.text: Sound travels faster through helium, raising the pitch of your voice
Helium shrinks your vocal cords temporarily
Helium makes your throat vibrate twice as fast

questions.fun_fact: Helium is far lighter than air, so sound waves zip through it much faster. This boosts the higher resonant tones your vocal tract amplifies, making your voice squeaky. Your vocal cords actually vibrate at the same rate as normal.

questions.question: Why does a stuck jar lid loosen more easily after you run it under hot water?

answers.text: The metal lid expands faster than the glass jar
The hot water dissolves the seal between lid and jar
The heat softens the metal so it stretches

questions.fun_fact: Metal expands more than glass for the same rise in temperature. Warming the lid makes it grow slightly larger in diameter than the glass neck beneath it, loosening the grip just enough to twist it free.

questions.question: Why do onions make you cry when you chop them?

answers.text: They release a gas that turns to mild acid on contact with your eyes
The smell triggers a reflex tear response in your nose
Tiny onion particles physically scratch the eye surface

questions.fun_fact: Cutting ruptures cells that mix enzymes and sulphur compounds, producing a volatile gas. When it reaches the watery film on your eyes it forms a small amount of sulfuric acid, and your tear glands flush to wash the irritant away.

questions.question: Why does ice float on water instead of sinking like most frozen solids?

answers.text: Water expands as it freezes, making ice less dense than liquid water
Trapped air bubbles make every ice cube lighter than water
Ice is colder, and cold objects always rise in liquid

questions.fun_fact: Most substances shrink and get denser when they solidify, but water's molecules lock into an open, spacious crystal lattice as they freeze. That makes ice about 9% less dense than liquid water, which is why lakes freeze top-down and fish survive winter beneath.

questions.question: Why does cutting a chilli pepper sometimes leave a burning sensation on your fingers for hours?

answers.text: Capsaicin is oily and clings to skin, triggering heat-sensing nerves
The pepper's acid slowly dissolves the top layer of skin
Pepper juice raises the actual temperature of your skin

questions.fun_fact: Capsaicin tricks the same nerve receptors that detect real heat, so your brain feels a burn with no actual temperature change. Because it's oil-based, water won't wash it off well, but fats like milk or oil dissolve and lift it away.

questions.question: Why does a hot-air balloon rise into the sky?

answers.text: Heated air inside is less dense than the cooler air outside
The burner produces a lighter-than-air gas called balloon gas
The fabric repels gravity once it reaches a high temperature

questions.fun_fact: Heating the air inside the envelope spreads its molecules apart, making that air lighter than the same volume of cool air around it. The balloon floats up for the same reason a cork rises in water, just with air instead of liquid.

questions.question: Why does a struck tuning fork keep humming a steady single note?

answers.text: Its two prongs vibrate at one fixed natural frequency
It contains a small electronic oscillator
The metal slowly releases stored sound it absorbed earlier

questions.fun_fact: A tuning fork's size and stiffness give it one dominant resonant frequency, so it rings out a pure, clean tone with almost no overtones. That purity is why musicians and instrument makers have used them as a tuning reference for over 300 years.

questions.question: Why does bread go stale even when you keep it sealed in a bag?

answers.text: Its starch molecules slowly recrystallise and squeeze out moisture
The bread keeps absorbing oxygen until it dries out
Bacteria eat the soft centre and harden the crust

questions.fun_fact: Staling isn't mainly about drying out. The gelatinised starch from baking gradually reorganises into a firmer crystal structure, a process called retrogradation, pushing water out of place. Oddly, the fridge speeds this up, which is why bread goes stale faster when refrigerated.

questions.question: Why do your fingers wrinkle after a long bath?

answers.text: Your nervous system actively shrinks blood vessels to pucker the skin
The skin swells as it soaks up water like a sponge
Soap strips away oils, causing the surface to collapse

questions.fun_fact: For a long time people assumed wrinkling was just swelling, but it's actually controlled by your nervous system constricting blood vessels under the skin. Researchers think the wrinkles act like rain treads, giving a better grip on wet objects.

questions.question: Why does a struck match suddenly burst into flame?

answers.text: Friction heat ignites chemicals on the match head
Striking releases compressed gas stored in the wood
The rough strip injects a spark of electricity

questions.fun_fact: Dragging the head across the rough strip generates heat through friction. On safety matches, that heat converts red phosphorus on the strip into a tiny bit of white phosphorus, which ignites instantly and sets off the match head's own chemicals.

questions.question: Why does a rainbow always appear in a curved arc?

answers.text: Raindrops bend light at one fixed angle, forming a circle of colour
The curve mirrors the round shape of the sun
Light bends around the curvature of the Earth

questions.fun_fact: Each raindrop sends sunlight back at about 42 degrees, so the bright band forms wherever drops sit at that angle from the anti-solar point, which traces a circle. From the ground you only see an arc, but from a plane a rainbow can appear as a full ring.

questions.question: Why does a struck bell or wine glass keep ringing long after you hit it?

answers.text: The whole object vibrates as one and loses energy slowly to the air
Sound echoes back and forth inside the hollow space
The metal generates fresh sound as it cools down

questions.fun_fact: A bell or glass is a resonant body that vibrates as a single unit at its natural frequency. It only sheds energy gradually by pushing the surrounding air, so the tone rings on. Touch it and you damp the vibration, silencing it at once.

questions.question: Why does a non-stick frying pan stop food from sticking?

answers.text: Its slippery coating barely lets other molecules bond to it
It stays cold in the centre so food never burns on
Microscopic holes blow out a constant cushion of steam

questions.fun_fact: The coating's molecules are remarkably unreactive, so almost nothing wants to grab hold of the surface, and even water beads off it. The same slick material is so non-stick that getting it to bond to the pan itself was the hard engineering problem.

questions.question: Why does the sky turn red and orange at sunset?

answers.text: Low sun angle means blue light scatters away, leaving red to reach you
The setting sun physically changes colour as it cools
Dust in the upper atmosphere glows red when heated

questions.fun_fact: At sunset, light skims a long path through the atmosphere. Air scatters blue light in all directions, so by the time the beam reaches you, mostly red and orange remain. The same scattering is why the daytime sky overhead looks blue.

questions.question: Why do soap bubbles show swirling rainbow colours on their surface?

answers.text: Light reflecting off the bubble's two thin surfaces interferes with itself
Soap contains dissolved dyes that spread across the film
The bubble splits white light like a tiny prism

questions.fun_fact: A bubble wall is incredibly thin, with light bouncing off both its inner and outer surface. The two reflections overlap and either reinforce or cancel certain colours depending on the film's thickness. As the bubble thins and drains, the colours shift and swirl.

questions.question: Why does cracking your knuckles make that popping sound?

answers.text: A gas bubble forms in the joint fluid and collapses
Two bones briefly knock together inside the joint
A tendon snaps over the edge of the bone

questions.fun_fact: Pulling the joint apart drops the pressure in the fluid until a gas-filled cavity forms, and the pop comes from that bubble's rapid collapse. It takes about 20 minutes for the gas to redissolve, which is why you can't immediately crack the same knuckle twice.

questions.question: Why does a freshly opened bottle of perfume fill a whole room with scent?

answers.text: Scent molecules evaporate and spread out to fill the space
Perfume gives off an invisible light that carries the smell
Warm air from your body sucks the scent across the room

questions.fun_fact: The fragrant molecules turn from liquid to vapour and then drift through the air, bumping randomly until they spread evenly through the room. This random spreading is called diffusion, and it's the same process that lets you smell coffee from another room.

questions.question: Why does a struck piano string keep playing its note until you lift your finger off the key?

answers.text: A felt damper rests on the string and only lifts while a key is held
The pianist's finger sends a continuous vibration into the key
The string is electrically charged while the key is pressed

questions.fun_fact: Each note has a felt damper that normally silences the string. Pressing a key lifts both the hammer and that damper, so the string rings freely; releasing the key drops the damper back to stop the sound. The sustain pedal lifts every damper at once.

questions.question: Why does a cut apple turn brown after a while?

answers.text: Exposed cells react with oxygen in the air
Light bleaches the natural colour out of the flesh
The apple starts to dry out and shrivel

questions.fun_fact: Cutting breaks cells and lets an enzyme in the apple meet oxygen, producing brown pigments much like the ones in tea. A splash of lemon juice slows it down because the acid and vitamin C interfere with that enzyme's reaction.

questions.question: What was the first song ever sung — and played — in space, by Gemini 6 astronauts in 1965?
questions.fun_fact: In December 1965, Gemini 6 astronauts Wally Schirra and Tom Stafford pranked Mission Control by reporting a UFO, then pulled out a harmonica and sleigh bells to play 'Jingle Bells' — the first instruments and song ever performed in space.

questions.question: What was the smartphone game Angry Birds originally inspired by in the news at the time?

answers.text: Swine flu and avian flu outbreaks

questions.fun_fact: Rovio designed the pigs as the enemy after the 2009 swine flu scare, and tied it to bird flu fears — that's why birds are angry at pigs. The simple sketch of wingless, legless round birds was chosen because it was instantly recognisable as an app icon.

questions.question: Why is the standard 'save' icon in software a floppy disk that most young users have never seen?

answers.text: It became a frozen convention before the disk went obsolete
Microsoft owns a trademark requiring its use
It was the first shape a computer mouse could draw

questions.fun_fact: The floppy-disk save icon became universal in 1990s software when disks were how you saved files. By the time disks vanished, the symbol was so deeply learned that replacing it would confuse users — so it survives as a 'skeuomorph' of dead technology.

questions.question: What does the 'M' in the MTV music channel logo officially stand for?
questions.fun_fact: MTV stands for Music Television. The very first music video it aired on 1 August 1981 was, fittingly, 'Video Killed the Radio Star' by The Buggles — a song about technology replacing an older medium.

questions.question: Where did the word 'paparazzi' for celebrity photographers come from?

answers.text: A character's surname in a Federico Fellini film
An Italian word for a swarm of insects
The brand of a popular 1950s camera

questions.fun_fact: In Fellini's 1960 film 'La Dolce Vita', a pushy news photographer is named Paparazzo. The name caught on, and the plural 'paparazzi' became the global word for aggressive celebrity photographers.

questions.question: What was the origin of the term 'spam' for unwanted bulk email?

answers.text: A repetitive Monty Python comedy sketch
An acronym for 'Sending Persistent Annoying Mail'
The name of the first email virus

questions.fun_fact: In a 1970 Monty Python sketch, a cafe menu features Spam in every dish and Vikings chant 'Spam, Spam, Spam' drowning out conversation. Early internet users borrowed it for messages that flood out everything else — that's why junk email is 'spam'.

questions.question: Why is a movie's pre-release publicity reel called a 'trailer'?

answers.text: Trailers originally played after the main film, not before
They were towed between cinemas on a trailer
They trailed off mid-scene to build suspense

questions.fun_fact: In the 1910s, promo reels for upcoming films were spliced to play at the END of the program, trailing after the feature. Audiences tended to leave, so studios moved them to the front — but the name 'trailer' stuck even though they now come first.

questions.question: What everyday kitchen appliance was invented after an engineer noticed a chocolate bar melting in his pocket?
questions.fun_fact: In 1945, Raytheon engineer Percy Spencer was standing near an active radar magnetron when a peanut chocolate bar in his pocket melted. He tested popcorn and an egg next, and the microwave oven was born — the first commercial model was nearly six feet tall.

questions.question: Where is the name of the snack food Pringles most often said to have come from?

answers.text: Pringle Drive, a street in Finneytown, Ohio

questions.fun_fact: Procter & Gamble staff reportedly picked the name from Pringle Drive, a street in Finneytown, Ohio, simply because it sounded good — though the company has never officially confirmed the story. The uniform saddle shape exists so the crisps stack without breaking — a packaging solution, not a flavour one.

questions.question: What was the children's modelling toy Play-Doh originally manufactured and sold as?
questions.fun_fact: The pliable compound was sold in the 1930s–40s to rub soot off wallpaper heated by coal stoves. When homes switched to gas heat and washable vinyl wallpaper, sales collapsed — until the maker's relative realised schoolchildren could mould it, and rebranded it as a toy in 1956.

questions.question: Why did the popular drink 7 Up originally have 'lithium' in some of its early formulations?

answers.text: It contained lithium citrate, marketed as a mood tonic
Lithium was used to carbonate the water
It was a misprint that the company never corrected

questions.fun_fact: Launched in 1929 as 'Bib-Label Lithiated Lemon-Lime Soda', early 7 Up contained lithium citrate, a mood-stabilising compound, and was pitched as a hangover and mood remedy. Lithium was removed from the recipe in 1948.

questions.question: What gave the colour 'magenta' its name?

answers.text: A bloody battle fought near the Italian town of Magenta

questions.fun_fact: The vivid dye was discovered in 1859, the same year as the Battle of Magenta in northern Italy. Makers named the new colour after the battle, which had just made headlines across Europe — the town's name now lives on in every printer ink cartridge.

questions.question: Where does the word 'denim', the fabric jeans are made from, come from?

answers.text: 'De Nîmes' — a sturdy cloth from Nîmes, France
A Dutch word for the colour blue
The surname of its inventor, Mr Denham

questions.fun_fact: 'Denim' is short for 'serge de Nîmes' — a sturdy cloth made in the city of Nîmes, France. 'Jeans' likewise comes from Genoa, Italy ('Gênes' in French), where a similar cotton fabric was made for sailors.

questions.question: What was the origin of the high-five gesture, according to the most-cited story?

answers.text: A spontaneous moment between two baseball players in 1977
An ancient Roman greeting between soldiers
A 1960s dance move on American Bandstand

questions.fun_fact: The most-cited origin is Dodgers outfielders Dusty Baker and Glenn Burke on 2 October 1977. Burke raised his hand to celebrate a home run, Baker slapped it, and the gesture spread from baseball into everyday life.

questions.question: Why do clocks and watches in advertisements almost always show a time around 10:10?

answers.text: The hands frame the logo and look like a smile
It is the exact time the first wristwatch was sold
Watchmaking law once required it for display models

questions.fun_fact: At roughly 10:10 the hands sit symmetrically, leave the brand name below the 12 unobscured, and form an upturned 'smile'. It's a deliberate marketing convention used by nearly every watch brand — look at any watch ad and you'll spot it.

questions.question: What was the original meaning of the word 'meme', decades before internet memes?

answers.text: A unit of cultural information that spreads like a gene
A French word for an inside joke
An early term for a photocopied flyer

questions.fun_fact: Biologist Richard Dawkins coined 'meme' in his 1976 book 'The Selfish Gene' to describe ideas, tunes and fashions that replicate and spread through culture the way genes spread through bodies. The internet just gave the concept a faster vehicle.

questions.question: Why is the wedding-ring finger the fourth finger on the left hand in many Western traditions?

answers.text: Ancient belief in a vein running directly to the heart
It was the only finger Roman law allowed rings on
It is the finger least used in farm labour

questions.fun_fact: The Romans believed a 'vena amoris', or vein of love, ran from the fourth finger straight to the heart. There's no such vein, but the romantic idea stuck for two thousand years and still places the ring there today.

questions.question: What was the toy Slinky originally being developed for when its inventor discovered it?

answers.text: A spring to stabilise ship instruments at sea
A mattress coil for the military

questions.fun_fact: Naval engineer Richard James was working on springs to keep sensitive shipboard instruments steady in 1943 when one fell off a shelf and 'walked' end over end. His wife Betty found the name 'Slinky' in a dictionary — it means sleek and sinuous.

questions.question: Why is the small pocket inside the right front pocket of most jeans there?

answers.text: It was originally made to hold a pocket watch
It was designed to hold a single coin for tolls
It was added to reinforce the seam and serves no use

questions.fun_fact: That tiny pocket dates to the 1870s and was built to protect a man's pocket watch on its chain. Levi's has called it the 'watch pocket'; over the years it's also held coins, matches, and tickets, long after watches moved to the wrist.

questions.question: What was the original purpose of Listerine when it was first sold in the late 1800s?

answers.text: A surgical antiseptic and floor cleaner

questions.fun_fact: Listerine launched in 1879 as a surgical antiseptic and was also sold to clean floors and treat gonorrhoea. It only became a mouthwash in the 1920s when marketers popularised the medical-sounding word 'halitosis' to make people anxious about bad breath.

questions.question: What is the real purpose of the loud 'clap' from a film clapperboard at the start of a take?

answers.text: It syncs the picture to separately recorded sound
It scares pigeons off outdoor sets
It signals the actors to begin their lines

questions.fun_fact: For most of film history, picture and sound were recorded on separate machines. The sharp 'clap' creates a single spike on the audio and a single frame where the sticks meet, letting editors line the two recordings up perfectly — that's its real job.

questions.question: What was the breakfast cereal Corn Flakes originally invented to promote?

answers.text: A bland diet meant to discourage unhealthy urges
A cheap food for circus animals

questions.fun_fact: John Harvey Kellogg ran a health sanitarium and believed plain food curbed harmful passions. He and his brother first stumbled on flaked cereal in 1894 while rolling out left-over boiled wheat, and went on to flake corn a few years later. His brother Will then added sugar and built the famous breakfast brand.

questions.question: What is the origin of the word 'OK'?

answers.text: A jokey 1830s newspaper abbreviation of 'oll korrect'
A naval flag signal meaning 'all clear'
A shortening of the inventor Otto Klein's initials

questions.fun_fact: 'OK' began as a fad in 1830s Boston newspapers for comically misspelled abbreviations — 'oll korrect' for 'all correct'. It got a huge boost from US President Martin Van Buren's 1840 campaign, nicknamed 'Old Kinderhook', and became one of the world's most recognised words.

questions.question: Why does the QWERTY keyboard layout scatter common letters instead of placing them in alphabetical order?

answers.text: To slow typists and stop early typewriter keys jamming
To match the order of telegraph Morse code
To make the inventor's surname typeable on the top row

questions.fun_fact: The 1870s layout separated frequently paired letters so the mechanical typebars of early machines wouldn't clash and jam. The jamming problem vanished long ago, but the layout was too entrenched to change — and you can still spell 'TYPEWRITER' using only the top row.

questions.question: Roughly how many copies has the printed Harry Potter book series sold worldwide?
questions.fun_fact: That makes it the best-selling book series in history, translated into more than 80 languages — including Ancient Greek, the longest text published in that language since antiquity.

questions.question: Why did the very first Pong arcade machine break down during its 1972 bar test?

answers.text: It was jammed completely full of coins
It overheated and caught fire within an hour
A frustrated customer kicked it over

questions.fun_fact: The machine at Andy Capp's Tavern stopped working because its coin box — a milk carton — overflowed. Atari realised the 'fault' was actually proof of staggering demand.

questions.question: Which 1902 film does this image come from?
questions.fun_fact: Georges Méliès was a stage magician before he made films. The rocket in the moon's eye is one of the oldest images almost everybody recognises without having seen the film.

questions.question: Which silent film star is shown here?
questions.fun_fact: Chaplin invented the Tramp in one afternoon in the costume department: trousers too wide, jacket too tight, shoes too big, and a cane. The character went on to appear in more than seventy films.

questions.question: Which character broke through in the 1928 film “Steamboat Willie”?
questions.fun_fact: “Steamboat Willie” was not the first Mickey Mouse film, but it was the first with synchronised sound — which is why it is the one everyone knows.

questions.question: Which 1922 film is this vampire from?
questions.fun_fact: The studio filmed Bram Stoker’s “Dracula” without buying the rights and changed the names. Stoker’s widow sued, a court ordered the copies destroyed, and the film survives only because prints had already left Germany.

questions.question: Which film movement does this 1920 poster belong to?
questions.fun_fact: “Das Cabinet des Dr. Caligari” was shot on painted sets: the crooked walls, the leaning houses and even the shadows on the floor were painted rather than lit.

questions.question: How many Oscars did Titanic win in 1998?
questions.fun_fact: Eleven — level with Ben Hur and The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King. Not one of them was for acting.

questions.question: How many episodes does the series Friends have in total?
questions.fun_fact: 236 episodes across ten seasons. In the final season each of the six leads earned a million dollars per episode, negotiated as a block and never individually.

questions.question: How many minutes long is the first Star Wars film from 1977?
questions.fun_fact: 121 minutes. The studio thought the film unsalvageable until Marcia Lucas and two colleagues recut it — the edit won an Oscar.

questions.question: How old was Macaulay Culkin when Home Alone was filmed?
questions.fun_fact: Ten. The film took nearly half a billion dollars worldwide and still holds the record for the highest-grossing live-action comedy.

questions.question: How many minutes long is Gone with the Wind?
questions.fun_fact: 238 minutes including overture and intermission. Adjusted for inflation it remains the highest-grossing film ever made.
